1.problem: \(ABC\) is an isosceles triangle with \(AB=2\) and \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\). \(D\) is the midpoint of \(BC\) and \(E\) is on \(AC\) such that the area of \(AEDB\) is twice the area of \(ECD\). Find the length of \(DE\).
1.solutions: Let \(F\) be the foot of the perpendicular from \(E\) to \(BC\). We have \[[AEDB]+[EDC]=[ABC]=2,\] so \([EDC]=2/3\). Since \[[EDC]=\frac12(EF)(DC),\] we get \(EF=FC=4/3\). Thus \(FD=1/3\), and by the Pythagorean Theorem, \[ED=\sqrt{\left(\frac43\right)^2+\left(\frac13\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{3}.\]

2.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with \(\angle A=90^\circ\), \(AB=1\), and \(AC=2\). Let \(\ell\) be a line through \(A\) perpendicular to \(BC\), and let the perpendicular bisectors of \(AB\) and \(AC\) meet \(\ell\) at \(E\) and \(F\), respectively. Find the length of segment \(EF\).
2.solutions: Let \(M,N\) be the midpoints of \(AB\) and \(AC\), respectively. We have \(\angle EAB=\angle ACB\), so \(\triangle AEM\sim\triangle CBA\) and \[AE=\frac{\sqrt5}{4}.\] Similarly, \(\angle FAC=\angle ABC\), so \(\triangle FAN\sim\triangle CBA\) and \(AF=\sqrt5\). Consequently, \[EF=AF-AE=\frac{3\sqrt5}{4}.\]

3.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with incenter \(I\). Let the circle centered at \(B\) and passing through \(I\) intersect side \(AB\) at \(D\) and let the circle centered at \(C\) passing through \(I\) intersect side \(AC\) at \(E\). Suppose \(DE\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(AI\). What are all possible measures of angle \(BAC\) in degrees?
3.solutions: Let \(\alpha=\angle BAC\). Since \(DE\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(AI\), we have \(DA=DI\), and \[\angle DIA=\angle DAI=\frac\alpha2.\] Also \(BD=BI\), so \(\angle IDB=\angle DIB=\alpha\). Hence \[\angle DBI=180^\circ-2\alpha,\] and therefore \(\angle ABC=360^\circ-4\alpha\). Similarly, \(\angle ACB=360^\circ-4\alpha\). Summing the angles of \(ABC\) gives \[720^\circ-7\alpha=180^\circ,\] so \(\alpha=540^\circ/7\).

4.problem: There are circles \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\). They intersect in two points, one of which is the point \(A\). \(B\) lies on \(\omega_1\) such that \(AB\) is tangent to \(\omega_2\). The tangent to \(\omega_1\) at \(B\) intersects \(\omega_2\) at \(C\) and \(D\), where \(D\) is the closer to \(B\). \(AD\) intersects \(\omega_1\) again at \(E\). If \(BD=3\) and \(CD=13\), find \(\frac{EB}{ED}\).
4.solutions: By power of a point, \[BA=\sqrt{BD\cdot BC}=\sqrt{3\cdot16}=4\sqrt3.\] Also \(\triangle DEB\sim\triangle DBA\), so \[\frac{EB}{ED}=\frac{BA}{BD}=\frac{4\sqrt3}{3}.\]

5.problem: A mouse lives in a circular cage with completely reflective walls. At the edge of this cage, a small flashlight with vertex on the circle whose beam forms an angle of \(15^\circ\) is centered at an angle of \(37.5^\circ\) away from the center. The mouse will die in the dark. What fraction of the total area of the cage can keep the mouse alive?
5.solutions:
We claim that, up to sets of area \(0\), the lit region is the entire cage except for the circle of half the cage’s radius centered at the center.

First, no part of this inner circle is lit. Along any reflected light path, every chord has the same length, so the minimum distance from the center to each chord is constant. None of the initial chords comes closer than half the cage’s radius to the center, so the concentric circle of half the radius remains dark.

It remains to show that every open subset of the outer region meets a light path. Choose a light path whose angle away from the center is irrational and whose first chord has midpoint at distance \(d\) from the center sufficiently close to the distance from the center to a point in the chosen open set. Every successive chord is a rotation of the first by an irrational angle, so these chords are dense among all chords at distance \(d\) from the center. Hence one passes through the open set. Thus any additional unlit portion outside the small circle has area \(0\).

The lit fraction is therefore \[1-\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac34.\]

6.problem:
Triangle \(ABC\) is an equilateral triangle with side length \(1\). Let \(X_0,X_1,\ldots\) be an infinite sequence of points such that the following conditions hold:

  • \(X_0\) is the center of \(ABC\).
  • For all \(i\ge0\), \(X_{2i+1}\) lies on segment \(AB\) and \(X_{2i+2}\) lies on segment \(AC\).
  • For all \(i\ge0\), \(\angle X_iX_{i+1}X_{i+2}=90^\circ\).
  • For all \(i\ge1\), \(X_{i+2}\) lies in triangle \(AX_iX_{i+1}\).

Find the maximum possible value of \[\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}|X_iX_{i+1}|,\] where \(|PQ|\) is the length of line segment \(PQ\).
6.solutions: Let \(Y\) be the foot of the perpendicular from \(A\) to \(X_0X_1\). The sum is \(X_0Y+YA\). Since \(AX_0=\sqrt3/3\) and \(\triangle AX_0Y\) is right, \[X_0Y+YA\le\sqrt2\,AX_0=\frac{\sqrt6}{3}.\] Equality is achieved when \(\angle YX_0A=45^\circ\), equivalently when \(\angle AX_1X_0=105^\circ\). Thus the maximum is \(\sqrt6/3\).

7.problem: Let \(S\) be the set of the points \((x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{2012})\) in \(2012\)-dimensional space such that \[|x_1|+|x_2|+\cdots+|x_{2012}|\le1.\] Let \(T\) be the set of points in \(2012\)-dimensional space such that \[\max_{i=1}^{2012}|x_i|=2.\] Let \(p\) be a randomly chosen point on \(T\). What is the probability that the closest point in \(S\) to \(p\) is a vertex of \(S\)?
7.solutions:
The set \(T\) is a hypercube boundary in \(2012\) dimensions containing the rotated hyperoctahedron \(S\). Fix a vertex \(v\) of \(S\). A point \(x\in T\) has \(v\) as its closest point of \(S\) precisely when \[(x-v)\cdot(w-v)\le0\] for every \(w\in S\). Because the condition is linear in \(w\), it suffices to check the other vertices of \(S\).

Without loss of generality take \(v=(1,0,\ldots,0)\). Checking \(w=(0,\pm1,0,\ldots,0)\) in every other coordinate gives \[1-x_1+x_i\le0,qquad1-x_1-x_i\le0\] for \(2\le i\le2012\). These conditions force \(x_1=2\) and \(x_i\in[-1,1]\) for every \(i\ge2\). Thus the favorable region for each vertex is a \(2011\)-dimensional cube of side length \(2\) on one face of \(T\).

There are \(2\cdot2012\) vertices and faces. Hence the favorable surface volume is \[2\cdot2012\cdot2^{2011},\] while the total surface volume is \[2\cdot2012\cdot4^{2011}.\] The probability is therefore \(1/2^{2011}\).

8.problem: Hexagon \(ABCDEF\) has a circumscribed circle and an inscribed circle. If \(AB=9\), \(BC=6\), \(CD=2\), and \(EF=4\), find \(\{DE,FA\}\).
8.solutions:
By Brianchon’s Theorem, \(AD,BE,CF\) concur at a point \(P\). Equal tangent lengths also give \[AB+CD+EF=BC+DE+FA.\] Let \(DE=x\), so \(FA=9-x\).

We have \(\triangle APB\sim\triangle EPD\), \(\triangle BPC\sim\triangle FPE\), and \(\triangle CPD\sim\triangle APF\). The second similarity gives \(BP/FP=3/2\), so write \(BP=3y\) and \(FP=2y\). The first similarity gives \(DP=xy/3\). The third then gives \[4y=\frac{(9-x)xy}{3},\] so \(x^2-9x+12=0\). Thus \[x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{33}}{2},\] and the unordered pair \(\{DE,FA\}\) is \[\left\{\frac{9+\sqrt{33}}{2},\frac{9-\sqrt{33}}{2}\right\}.\]

9.problem: Let \(O,O_1,O_2,O_3,O_4\) be points such that \(O_1,O,O_3\) and \(O_2,O,O_4\) are collinear in that order, \(OO_1=1\), \(OO_2=2\), \(OO_3=\sqrt2\), \(OO_4=2\), and \(\angle O_1OO_2=45^\circ\). Let \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4\) be the circles with respective centers \(O_1,O_2,O_3,O_4\) that go through \(O\). Let \(A\) be the intersection of \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\), \(B\) be the intersection of \(\omega_2\) and \(\omega_3\), \(C\) be the intersection of \(\omega_3\) and \(\omega_4\), and \(D\) be the intersection of \(\omega_4\) and \(\omega_1\), with \(A,B,C,D\) all distinct from \(O\). What is the largest possible area of a convex quadrilateral \(P_1P_2P_3P_4\) such that \(P_i\) lies on \(\omega_i\) and that \(A,B,C,D\) all lie on its perimeter?
9.solutions:
First maximize the area of \(\triangle P_1OP_2\); the quadrilateral’s area is the sum of this and the three analogous triangle areas. If \(A\ne P_1,P_2\), then angle relations on the two circles give \[\triangle OO_1P_1\sim\triangle OO_2P_2.\] This spiral similarity implies \(\angle P_1OP_2=\angle O_1OO_2\), which is fixed. By the sine area formula, the area is maximized by maximizing \(OP_1OP_2\), so \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) should be diametrically opposite \(O\) on their circles. The same reasoning applies to \(P_3,P_4\).

For these choices, \(A,B,C,D\) lie on the quadrilateral because the corresponding angles are right. Its area is \[\frac12\sin45^\circ\cdot4\left(1\cdot2+2\cdot\sqrt2+\sqrt2\cdot2+2\cdot1\right) =8+4\sqrt2.\]

10.problem:
Let \(\mathcal C\) denote the set of points \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\) such that \(x^2+y^2\le1\). A sequence \((A_i=(x_i,y_i))_{i\ge0}\) of points in \(\mathbb R^2\) is ‘centric’ if it satisfies the following properties:

  • \(A_0=(x_0,y_0)=(0,0)\), \(A_1=(x_1,y_1)=(1,0)\).
  • For all \(n\ge0\), the circumcenter of triangle \(A_nA_{n+1}A_{n+2}\) lies in \(\mathcal C\).

Let \(K\) be the maximum value of \(x_{2012}^2+y_{2012}^2\) over all centric sequences. Find all points \((x,y)\) such that \(x^2+y^2=K\) and there exists a centric sequence such that \(A_{2012}=(x,y)\).
10.solutions:
Consider any triangle \(A_nA_{n+1}A_{n+2}\) with circumcenter \(P_n\). By the triangle inequality, \[A_nP_n\le A_nA_0+A_0P_n\le A_nA_0+1.\] Since \(P_nA_n=P_nA_{n+2}\), \[A_{n+2}A_0\le P_nA_{n+2}+1=A_nP_n+1\le A_nA_0+2.\] Therefore \[\sqrt{x_{n+2}^2+y_{n+2}^2}\le\sqrt{x_n^2+y_n^2}+2.\] Equality holds exactly when \(A_n,A_0,P_n,A_{n+2}\) are collinear and \(P_n\) lies on the unit circle. Iterating gives \[\sqrt{x_{2012}^2+y_{2012}^2}\le2012,\] so \(K=2012^2\).

For equality, \(P_0\) must lie on the unit circle and on the perpendicular bisector \(x=1/2\) of \(A_0A_1\). Thus \[P_0=\left(\frac12,\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right).\] Taking the positive choice, equality forces \(A_2=(1,\sqrt3)\). Inductively, \[P_{2n}=\left(\frac{(-1)^n}{2},\frac{(-1)^n\sqrt3}{2}\right), \qquad A_{2n}=(-1)^{n+1}(n,n\sqrt3).\] The intervening odd-indexed points can be chosen so that all required circumcenters lie in \(\mathcal C\). Hence \[A_{2012}=(-1006,1006\sqrt3).\] The negative initial choice reflects the entire construction across the \(x\)-axis, giving the other point. Therefore the answer is \[\{(-1006,1006\sqrt3),(-1006,-1006\sqrt3)\}.\]
